paragraphs: This story begins with its hero’s death. Silas Deemer died on 16 July 1863 and was buried two days later. Every man, woman and older child in the village had known him personally, so the funeral, as the local newspaper put it, “was well attended.” Following the custom of that time and place, the coffin was opened beside the grave. All the assembled friends and neighbours filed past for a last look at the dead man’s face. Then, before everyone’s eyes, Silas Deemer was lowered into the ground. Some eyes were a little misty. Generally speaking, however, the burial lacked neither observance nor observation. Silas was undoubtedly dead, and no one could have pointed to any failure of ritual that would justify his return from the grave. Yet if human testimony is worth anything—and it certainly once put an end to witchcraft in and around Salem—he returned.

I forgot to mention that Silas Deemer died and was buried in the little village of Hillbrook, where he had lived for thirty-one years. He had been what certain parts of the Union, admittedly a free country, call a “merchant.” In other words, he kept a shop selling the sort of things usually sold in shops of that kind. As far as anyone knew, his honesty had never been questioned, and everyone respected him highly. The most critical person could have held only one thing against him: he paid too much attention to business. Yet no one did hold it against him, although many others who showed no greater devotion were judged less kindly. The business Silas attended to was mostly his own. Perhaps that made a difference.

At Deemer’s death, no one could remember a single day, except Sundays, that he had not spent in his “store” since opening it more than twenty-five years earlier. His health had been perfect throughout that time, and he could see no merit in any reason anyone offered, or might offer, to lure him away from his counter. Once, the story goes, he was summoned to the county town as a witness in an important case but failed to appear. The lawyer bold enough to propose that he be “reprimanded” was solemnly told that the Court regarded the suggestion with “surprise.” Judicial surprise is not an emotion lawyers usually wish to provoke. The proposal was hastily withdrawn, and the two sides agreed on what Mr Deemer would have said had he been there. The opposing side pressed its advantage as far as possible, making this imaginary testimony decidedly harmful to those who had wanted him as a witness. In brief, the whole region regarded Silas Deemer as Hillbrook’s one immovable certainty. Moving him anywhere else would bring some gloomy public misfortune or violent calamity.

Mrs Deemer and two grown daughters lived in the rooms upstairs. But Silas had never been known to sleep anywhere except on a cot behind the shop counter. There, quite by accident, someone found him dying one night. He passed away just before it was time to take down the shutters. Although unable to speak, he seemed conscious. Those who knew him best thought that, if the end had unfortunately been delayed beyond the usual opening time, the effect on him would have been deplorable.

Such was Silas Deemer, and so fixed and unvarying were his life and habits, that the village humorist—who had once attended college—gave him the nickname “Old Ibidem”, or “Old In-the-Same-Place”. In the newspaper’s first issue after his death, the humorist explained, without giving offence, that Silas had taken “a day off.” It lasted more than a day. But the record suggests that well before a month had passed, Mr Deemer made it clear he had no time to be dead.

One of Hillbrook’s most respected citizens was Alvan Creede, a banker. He lived in the finest house in town, kept a carriage, and was admirable in various other ways. He knew something of the advantages of travel too. He had often visited Boston and, people believed, had once been to New York, although he modestly denied that glittering distinction. I mention it only to help explain Mr Creede’s worth. Either way it did him credit: to his intelligence if he had exposed himself, even briefly, to metropolitan culture; to his honesty if he had not.

One pleasant summer evening, at about ten o’clock, Mr Creede entered his garden gate and walked up the gravel path, which looked very white in the moonlight. He climbed the stone steps of his fine house, paused, and put his key in the lock. As he pushed the door open, he met his wife crossing the passage from the sitting room to the library. She greeted him pleasantly, pulled the door farther back, and held it for him to enter. Instead, he turned, looked around his feet outside the threshold, and exclaimed in surprise.
“Why—what the devil,” he said, “has happened to that jug?”
“What jug, Alvan?” his wife asked, without much sympathy.
“A jug of maple syrup. I carried it home from the shop and set it down here to open the door. What the—”

“There, there, Alvan. Please don’t swear again,” she interrupted. Hillbrook, incidentally, is not the only place in the Christian world where a lingering belief in more than one god forbids taking the Evil One’s name in vain.
The jug of maple syrup that the relaxed customs of village life had allowed Hillbrook’s leading citizen to carry home from the shop was not there.
“Are you quite sure, Alvan?”
“My dear, do you think a man doesn’t know when he’s carrying a jug? I bought that syrup at Deemer’s as I passed. Deemer himself filled the jug and lent it to me, and I—”

That sentence remains unfinished to this day. Mr Creede staggered into the house, entered the sitting room, and dropped into an armchair, trembling in every limb. He had suddenly remembered that Silas Deemer had been dead for three weeks.
Mrs Creede stood beside her husband, watching him with surprise and anxiety.
“For Heaven’s sake,” she said, “what’s wrong with you?”

Since Mr Creede’s trouble had no obvious connection with the interests of Heaven, he apparently saw no need to explain it at that request. He said nothing, merely stared. Long moments of silence passed, broken only by the clock’s steady ticking. It seemed a little slower than usual, as though politely allowing them extra time to recover their senses.

“Jane, I’ve gone mad. That’s it.” He spoke thickly and quickly. “You should have told me. You must have noticed my symptoms before they became so obvious that I noticed them myself. I thought I was passing Deemer’s shop. It was open and lit up—that’s what I thought. Of course it’s never open now. Silas Deemer stood at his desk behind the counter. My God, Jane, I saw him as clearly as I see you. I remembered you saying you wanted maple syrup, so I went in and bought some. That’s all. I bought two quarts of maple syrup from Silas Deemer, who is dead and underground, but who nevertheless drew that syrup from a cask and handed it to me in a jug. He talked to me too, rather gravely, I remember—even more gravely than usual. But I can’t remember a word he said. Yet I saw him. Good Lord, I saw him and spoke to him, and he’s dead! So I thought—but I’m mad, Jane, as crazy as a beetle, and you’ve kept it from me.”
This speech gave the woman time to collect what wits she had.

“Alvan,” she said, “believe me, you’ve shown no sign of insanity. This was certainly an illusion. What else could it be? That would be too terrible! But you’re not insane. You’re working too hard at the bank. You shouldn’t have gone to the directors’ meeting tonight. Anyone could see you were ill. I knew something would happen.”

He may have thought the prophecy had been a little slow, waiting for the event before appearing. But he said nothing about that, being concerned with his own condition. He was calm now and could think clearly.

“Undoubtedly the phenomenon was subjective,” he said, making a rather ridiculous switch to scientific jargon. “Even if we grant that a spirit can appear and take material form, a half-gallon brown clay jug is another matter. A piece of heavy, coarse pottery appearing and taking shape out of nothing—that is hardly conceivable.”

As he finished, a child ran into the room: his little daughter, wearing a nightdress. She hurried to him, threw her arms around his neck, and said, “Naughty Papa, you forgot to come and kiss me! We heard you open the gate, so we got up and looked out. And, Papa dear, Eddy wants to know if he can have the little jug when it’s empty.”
As Alvan Creede understood the full meaning of this revelation, he visibly shuddered. The child could not have heard a word of their conversation.

Silas Deemer’s estate was in the hands of an administrator who thought it best to sell the “business.” The shop had therefore remained closed since its owner’s death. Another “merchant” had bought all its goods as a single lot and taken them away. The rooms upstairs were empty too, since the widow and daughters had moved to another town.

On the evening after Alvan Creede’s adventure, which had somehow “got out,” a crowd of men, women and children filled the pavement opposite the shop. Every Hillbrook resident now knew it was haunted by the late Silas Deemer, although many pretended not to believe it. The boldest of these, generally the youngest, threw stones at the front of the building, the only accessible side. They carefully avoided the windows, whose shutters were off. Disbelief had not yet become malice. A few adventurous people crossed the road and rattled the door in its frame, struck matches and held them near the window, and tried to see into the dark interior. Some spectators drew attention to their wit by shouting, groaning and challenging the ghost to a footrace.

After a considerable time passed without any manifestation, and many people had left, everyone remaining began to notice a dim yellow light spreading through the shop. At once all demonstrations stopped. The fearless souls at the door and windows retreated across the street and disappeared into the crowd. The small boys stopped throwing stones. No one spoke above a whisper. They whispered excitedly and pointed to the steadily growing light. No one could have guessed how long it had been since the first faint glow appeared. Eventually, however, the light was bright enough to reveal the entire shop. There, standing at his desk behind the counter, Silas Deemer was clearly visible!

The effect on the crowd was extraordinary. It rapidly melted away at both edges as the timid departed. Many ran as fast as their legs could carry them. Others left with greater dignity, occasionally looking back over a shoulder. At last twenty or more people, mostly men, remained where they stood, speechless, staring and excited. The apparition inside paid them no attention. It seemed occupied with an account book.

Soon three men left the crowd as if moved by a shared impulse and crossed the street. One, a heavy man, was about to put his shoulder against the door when it opened, apparently without human help. The brave investigators entered. The moment they crossed the threshold, the awed watchers outside saw them behaving in the strangest way. They held their hands out in front of them, wandered along crooked routes, and collided violently with the counter, boxes and barrels on the floor, and one another. They turned awkwardly this way and that, seeming to try to escape but unable to retrace their steps. Their exclamations and curses were audible. Yet the apparition of Silas Deemer showed no interest in any of it.

No one afterwards remembered what impulse moved the crowd. But the whole mass—men, women, children and dogs—rushed for the entrance together in a tumult. They jammed the doorway, pushing to get ahead, until they finally formed a line and advanced step by step. Through some subtle spiritual or physical alchemy, watching had turned into action. The sightseers had become part of the spectacle. The audience had seized the stage.

To the only spectator left across the street, the banker Alvan Creede, the shop and the crowd pouring into it remained fully lit. He could clearly see every strange thing happening inside. But to those within, everything was pitch-black. It was as though each person, on being pushed through the doorway, had been struck blind and driven frantic by it. They groped aimlessly, tried to force their way out against the crowd, pushed and elbowed, struck at random, fell and were trampled, then rose and trampled others in turn. They seized one another’s clothes, hair and beards. They fought like animals, cursed, shouted, and called one another insulting and obscene names. Finally, when Alvan Creede had watched the last person in the line enter that dreadful turmoil, the light suddenly went out. Everything became as black to him as it was to those inside. He turned away and left.

Early the next morning, a curious crowd gathered around “Deemer’s.” Some had fled the night before but now possessed the courage of sunshine. Others were honest people on their way to work. The shop door stood open. The place was empty, but there were scraps of clothing and tangles of hair on the walls, floor and furniture. Hillbrook’s warriors had somehow pulled themselves free and gone home to treat their injuries and swear they had spent the whole night in bed. On the dusty desk behind the counter lay the sales book. Its entries, in Deemer’s handwriting, stopped on 16 July, the last day of his life. There was no record of a later sale to Alvan Creede.

That is the whole story, except that once people’s passions had cooled and reason had resumed its age-old rule, Hillbrook admitted something. Considering how harmless and honourable Silas Deemer’s first commercial transaction under his new circumstances had been, the deceased might properly have been allowed to resume business at his old premises without being mobbed. The local historian, from whose unpublished work these facts are taken, was thoughtful enough to record his agreement with that judgment.
